name: Benzatropine
lead: Benzatropine (benztropine, sold as Cogentin) is an anticholinergic prescription medicine used to ease tremor, stiffness and muscle spasms in Parkinson's disease and to treat movement side effects of antipsychotic drugs [1]. Its appearance relevance is through those effects: it can settle visible tremor, involuntary facial or neck muscle contractions and, in some cases, drooling and salivary gland swelling caused by other medicines [2][1].
It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, restoring balance with dopamine signalling, and may also affect dopamine reuptake [1]. It has been used for more than 50 years [1].
Published evidence includes reviews of dystonia and Parkinson's treatment and a case report with systematic review on clozapine-induced parotid swelling [3][4][2].

chain: Calms drug-induced tremor, dystonia and drooling
Steadier, more natural facial and body movement
angle.text: Benzatropine is used to relieve visible side effects of antipsychotics such as facial muscle spasms, tremor and hypersalivation. Its appearance benefit is restoring ordinary movement and expression where these effects are present.

card.summary: An anticholinergic prescription drug that relieves tremor, muscle spasms and drug-induced drooling, restoring steadier movement and expression.
card.note: Prescription-only; anticholinergic effects include heat intolerance, confusion and urinary retention.

quick.overview:
Benzatropine is an older anticholinergic prescription drug. Doctors use it to reduce tremor and rigidity in Parkinson's disease and to treat muscle spasms, restlessness and stiffness caused by antipsychotics.

Appearance-related uses are indirect: calmer facial and neck muscles, less tremor, and in some reports less drooling or salivary gland swelling.
quick.mechanism: It competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system, offsetting the excess cholinergic activity that follows dopamine blockade, and has antihistamine properties as well [1].
quick.risks: Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, reduced sweating with overheating risk, and memory or confusion problems; long-term anticholinergic use has been linked to cognitive risks. It is prescription-only.

paras: Benzatropine has no direct cosmetic role. In a published case, benzatropine combined with terazosin resolved painful parotid swelling and hypersalivation caused by clozapine, a visible facial change [2].
It is used for Parkinson's disease, drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia and parkinsonism, and sometimes off-label for dystonia and drooling [1][3][4].
It antagonizes muscarinic receptors and crosses the blood-brain barrier; it is structurally related to atropine and has antihistamine activity [1].

Reported effects include anhidrosis, hyperthermia and cognitive impairment, and caution is advised with glaucoma or prostatic enlargement [1]. Anticholinergic burden in people with schizophrenia has itself been the subject of a registered study [5].

A BMJ Clinical Evidence review covers dystonia treatments [3], and a review addresses alternatives to levodopa in early Parkinson's disease [4]. A systematic review and case describe benzatropine for clozapine-related parotid swelling [2]. Benztropine was tested for cocaine craving in a registered phase 2 trial [6]. A WHO database analysis examined drug-related catatonia in youths [7].
